#3565. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

New heroes and villains are still joining James Gunn's DC Universe franchise.

While it was revealed earlier in November that Gunn and Peter Safran will be stepping down as DC Studios co-CEOs, the DCU's Chapter 1: "Gods and Monsters" slate is continuing, as there are still projects in the works that have yet to be released. With various live-action and animated films and TV shows in different stages of production, one of them recently found its titular lead.

In a new interview with the Happy, Sad, Confused podcast, Josh Hutcherson finally broke his silence on being cast as Scott Free in the animated Mister Miracle series, which will also star Mackenzie Davis as Big Barda. When he was first asked if it has already been recorded, he excitedly shared, "We have! It's awesome," before elaborating on how he landed the DCU gig, while also confirming whether he would play the titular hero in live-action.

"This was like a very extensive auditioning process, because whoever plays them in the animated version will play them in the live-action version. So that's the plan. That's the track that we're trying to follow," the Hunger Games star stated, while adding, "Since I didn't get cast in Spider-Man, I was like, 'I don't ever want to be a superhero. Like, it's fine. I never really wanted that.’" However, things changed once the DC opportunity was given to him.

Hutcherson went on to say, "And then Mister Miracle came around, and I read, all I had was like a few of the scenes to do the audition, and it was such a cool character. I started getting into the comics and reading through those, and the world is amazing. What it talks about with mental health and all of that, I think it's something that's very special. Josh Hutcherson: "But Tom King, who wrote the comics, is phenomenal. He was our showrunner as well, so he knows it inside and out. He knows Scott Free/Mister Miracle inside and out. And getting to have Mackenzie Davis there with me as well to play Big Barda, she was amazing. And that was just such a great project."

While Gunn and Safran will be replaced by Jeremy Latcham, who will start as DC Studios' new CEO on December 1, the Guardians of the Galaxy trilogy director did stress in his statement that characters they set up during their time will continue. And, of course, the characters we set up will live on. Thank you so very, very much for embracing the characters and stories we've put on screen."

While there may not be any announced plans right now for when Mister Miracle and Big Barda will appear in live-action, it will depend on what happens to the franchise as a whole. Assuming that there won't be another reboot, if the animated show becomes a success, there are multiple ways for upcoming DCU movies to utilize the characters after their small-screen debut.

#3561. Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

At the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic says Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

#3559. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3558. Watch the ‘Backrooms’ VFX Supervisor Explain His Unique Process of Collaborating with Kane Parsons

When you hire a 20-year-old director to adapt his own viral YouTube series into a major Hollywood film, you’re not going to end up with a traditional movie. That’s part of what made Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms” such a massive critical and commercial success for A24. Audiences were eager to embrace Parsons as a major new filmmaking voice — and his crew members were just as excited for the chance to work with him.

During IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “Backrooms” VFX Supervisor Edward Douglas broke down the unique workflow that he developed with Parsons during pre-production. He explained that Parsons was used to making his own effects in Blender, so the team started communicating with him using the popular VFX software. Related Stories Aaron Pierre on ‘Lanterns,’ the DC Shake-Up, and Landing a Role in Ryan Gosling’s ‘Star Wars’ Movie Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’

“The first conversation I had with Kane Parsons was ‘How do you like to work?’ And we embraced his process,” Douglas said. “Because his way of communicating with the entire crew was first, through Blender. He built 100,000 square feet of sets in Blender and passed it off to the production designer. And it immediately crashed his computer. But that let us start breaking down everything.”

Despite costing less than $10 million, “Backrooms” contained a significant number of VFX shots. Douglas explained that the process became a unique mix of traditional effects work by seasoned pros and found-footage-style shots that Parsons did himself.

“It was an indie budget film, but it had over ten minutes of full CG,” Douglas said. “Some of it was traditional, and some of it was Backrooms found footage exploration. That ended up being a hybrid VFX process. We had very traditional sequences when we were working with VFX Blenders. And then we had more of our Kane Parsons DIY pipeline for scenes that he would really be touching himself. And we set it up so that Kane could actually log into the VFX Blender servers and tweak things, set up shots. Because that was his way. He could say, ‘Here are the notes,’ or Can I show you?’ And we’d want to create a way for him to show us. Because he is, at his heart, a VFX artist.”

#3557. Report: iPhone set to gain market share in 2027 amid industry-wide slump

Apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a new report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a new Morgan Stanley research report says Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which launched only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

Back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That said, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

When it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it launched, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less important in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3554. 10 Years Before The Boys, This 37-Part Sci-Fi Series Perfected The Anti-Superhero Formula

Memory Ngulube joined Screen Rant in April 2024 as part of the Movies and TV team. Since then, she has written for the Perennials and Streaming team, covering a wide range of topics from new releases to old movies and TV shows. Memory is currently a Classic TV writer.  Before joining Screen Rant, Memory was a freelance copywriter who specialized in email marketing and social media management. While she enjoyed her job, her true passion was always movies and TV. When she isn’t writing for Screen Rant, Memory can be found reading, baking (which is one of her passions), or watching her favorite K-drama.

Nearly a decade before The Boys dismantled the idea that people with superpowers need to be morally flawless, a 37-episode series showed that sometimes it's more entertaining when characters are anything but heroic. Of course, the culture surrounding superheroes that The Boys has created cannot be overstated, especially as diabolical shows become increasingly popular these days. However, it's not even the first series to do so, even if it is arguably the most graphic, violent, and downright strange.

Premiering in 2009, Misfits was a superhero series that had little interest in making its characters aspirational. The show followed a group of young offenders sentenced to community service who are caught in a bizarre electrical storm and suddenly develop supernatural abilities. These superpowered individuals are far from the MCU's Avengers. Instead, they engage in questionable behavior, just like the characters in The Boys.

Misfits consistently challenged the idea that superheroes need to be conventional. The series was unapologetically crude and has a British sense of humor that fans of The Boys can appreciate. Unfortunately, Misfits is not as recognizable today as it was when it aired, but it deserves its flowers for changing how superheroes are presented to audiences.

The 2000s were a treasure trove of excellent TV shows, with many from that era, like Deadwood, Breaking Bad, and Fringe, still held in high regard today. Unfortunately, not all were lucky enough to become cultural phenomena. Nevertheless, the influence of shows such as Misfits is still evident in modern TV.

While villains in superhero series have been a staple for decades, unconventional superpowered people have not. Misfits did not pull any punches when it came to showing its characters in all their messy glory. The heroes had difficult lives and personal struggles. So, understandably, when they got their powers, they weren't rushing to save the world. Prime Video’s Invincible and The Boys, in particular, have proved time and again that audiences relate more to flawed characters than to protagonists like the perfect Captain America.

A critically acclaimed sitcom with a 100% Rotten Tomatoes score is the perfect palate cleanser for anyone exhausted by the MCU and the DCU.

Interestingly, Misfits never relies exclusively on the usual flying, super-strength, or laser-beam abilities. The superpowers in the show, such as immortality, invisibility, and sexual manipulation, are weird and, at times, deeply unsettling. The powers often create more problems than they solve, letting Misfits explore human flaws in waystraditional superhero shows rarely do.

Misfits has a lot of good things going for it, but its cast is arguably the best. Most of the actors in the show are pretty familiar, given that they’ve gone on to star in famous TV shows. For example, Robert Sheehan, who steals scenes as Nathan Young in Misfits with his obnoxious and sometimes annoying personality, went on to star in another superhero series, The Umbrella Academy, as well as Mortal Engines and Love/Hate.

The Umbrella Academy, Love/Hate, The Mortal Instruments: City of Bones

Lovesick, The Good Doctor, Agatha Christie's Tommy & Tuppence

Iwan Rheon, known for his role as Game of Thrones' most hated character (aside from Joffrey), Ramsay Bolton, plays Simon Bellamy, a socially awkward characteralmost as strange as his GoT counterpart. Lauren Socha, Antonia Thomas, and Nathan Stewart-Jarrett also helped establish the original group's dynamic. Even as Misfits introduced new characters and underwent significant cast changes, it continued to benefit from performers who understood the show's unconventional tone.

Rheon isn't the only Game of Thrones alum spotted in Misfits: Michelle Fairley, who portrayed Catelyn Stark in the high fantasy series, plays Louise Young, Nathan’s mother, while Nathalie Emmanuel (Missandei), Ellie Kendrick (Meera Reed), Josef Altin (Pypar), and Gwyneth Keyworth (Clea) also appear. Misfits cast is full of incredible actors and characters who work well together, despite their contrasting and sometimes clashing personalities. More often than not, a cast can break or make a show, and fortunately, Misfits’ is perfect.

Misfits is a British comedy-drama sci-fi series that blends science fiction with dark comedy. It is centered around five young offenders who gain supernatural abilities after a bizarre electrical storm. Set during their community service, the show explores how each character deals with their newfound powers, shining a light on the darker sides of having special abilities.

#3553. WhatsApp’s first-party chat history backup service moves ahead

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp users running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Users can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot currently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app update.

#3551. Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation

Film is always a collaborative medium, but one of the special things about animation is that you can craft incredibly nuanced performances with people who never get to meet. Voice acting in animation is a discipline in its own right — as legends like Mel Blanc and Eric Bauza show — where actors impart a kind of electric energy that carries through into the art style of what they’re voicing. So is voice directing. And the secret to both is in providing foundations for animators to build something bigger.

“Wildwood” director Travis Knight did a lot of the directing of his voice cast in lockdown Zooms, and hodge-podge recording setups, where it can be hard to remember that you’re developing something that needs to spiritually connect to the animation, whether existing animatics already exist or not. There isn’t the same kind of immersiveness for actors that live-action sets, costumes, and the basic pleasure of getting to read lines against other actors all provide. They have to build it from scratch. Related Stories Watch the ‘Backrooms’ VFX Supervisor Explain His Unique Process of Collaborating with Kane Parsons Aaron Pierre on ‘Lanterns,’ the DC Shake-Up, and Landing a Role in Ryan Gosling’s ‘Star Wars’ Movie

“It asks something very different of an actor, which is challenging because an actor can bring so much to performance before they even utter a word,” Knight told IndieWire on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “So when you cast these things, it’s really interesting because sometimes the things we love about actors are not their voice; it’s everything else. So we will always listen, we’ll take clips from actors’ other films and their interviews, and we’ll put them against a design of a character.”

Hearing a voice against a design can be revelatory, Knight believes, because it can teach a director and an animation team about who a character really is, whether a performer is really going to work or not, even before they step into the booth. It’s also an important way to help sort the whole of an ensemble so that actors occupy different aural frequencies and accents, and don’t sound too similar. You want to really be able to feel the difference between Carey Mulligan’s powerfully sinister Alexandra and Angela Bassett’s regal General.

And then, once the voice cast is in the booth, it’s also on the director and the team to help each voice actor sketch out all the different permutations of emotion the animators will then use as inspiration, and as tools.

“You’ll get the scene 30, 40, 50 different ways,” Knight said. “It takes forever. But, in the end, if you can do it properly, it feels like these characters are living in the same scene at the same time. And then it comes down to the animator to try to figure out how they can match the beauty of the vocal performance with the physical performance.”

That’s the normal process for feature animation: finding compelling voices, matching them with a design that feels spiritually connected to that voice, covering the performance many different ways, and then assembling a template for animators to build off of. And it’s the director, really, who has to hold in their head the many ways that the disparate parts will all come together.

“An animator is an actor, but they’re just acting through their hands and through a puppet, and it’s two actors collaborating to create a complete performance. But oftentimes it happens across space, across time. And when it comes together in a harmonious way, it’s really beautiful because this thing seems like it’s completely alive,” Knight said.

But sometimes, voice actors’ performances do get to be alive together. That was a key creative choice that director Leah Nelson made for “Tangles” — it’s hard to argue with the logic of putting Abbi Jacobson, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, and Bryan Cranston all in a room together to act out an earnest family drama, even if there’s a bit of mic bleed.

“I’m so glad we [put them together]. And it wasn’t that hard. It took a little bit of scheduling Tetris to get it done, but it was so worthwhile,” Nelson told IndieWire. “Abbi does a ton of voice work, and often they’re alone and not even able to have someone to read against them. Sometimes they’re just doing the lines and sort of jumping around. And what I ultimately wanted was to have this really naturalistic dialogue.”

“Tangles” boasts naturalism when it comes to sound, from bespoke foley to overlapping banter that isn’t meant to be precisely understood but to convey the chaos of one’s own (infuriating, loving) family. So Nelson and her team embraced the ways actors can build on each other, and even on improv, in recording the dialogue.

“A lot of humor came out of giving them time to not only play with the dialogue but to play with each other. But also, those really intimate and difficult moments of the film, they could look in each other’s eyes and work through those moments. That was important to me, and it was important to them as well. So it was an experience we all went through together.”

The one downside of treating recording sessions more like the rehearsals for a play is the risk of wrecking takes. “We spent a lot of time at the table trying to hold [our reactions] in or like, ‘Don’t sneeze! Nobody move!’” Nelson joked. “But I didn’t want it to sound like there was so much suturing; the mastery of the dialogue editing to make it all sound naturalistic, so we also did a lot of work to make that happen. But what we had to work with felt very naturalistic to begin with.”

The ultimate example of naturalistic voice acting, however, might be on display in “Wildwood.” Knight’s own son was a newborn while the team was laying down track for the film, which made him the perfect actor for the role of kidnapped Baby Mac.

“I essentially chased him around the house with a digital recorder. Sometimes with my iPhone. I was just trying to coax things out of him, make him laugh and giggle and verbalize. And the thing about babies is that they’re constantly trying to make sense of the world,” Knight said. “They’re always babbling and trying to make shapes with their mouths. So we have a lot of that babbling in the movie, and it helped make it feel naturalistic.”

It speaks to the wide-ranging power of voice acting in animation: you can get to naturalism through a grounded collaboration between actors, an actor in complete isolation, or hitting “record” on an iPhone while you’re changing a diaper.

“Wildwood” is now in theaters. “Tangles” releases in theaters on January 15, 2027.

#3550. iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%

Percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

#3549. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3548. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3547. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3545. Bill Hader’s Feature Directorial Debut ‘They Know’ Lands at Black Bear

Bill Hader‘s first film as a director has found its distribution partner. Black Bear has acquired North American distribution rights to “They Know,” Hader’s upcoming psychological horror film that he co-stars in with Linda Cardellini. The growing distributor, which just released “Wicker” nationwide, acquired the rights from financier MRC in what was described as a competitive situation.

Per an official synopsis, “They Know” follows a divorced dad who becomes increasingly suspicious and paranoid that his ex-wife’s new mysterious partner is exerting a strange, unsettling influence on their children.

“Bill Hader is a singular talent both in front of and behind the camera, and he has delivered a film in ‘They Know’ unlike anything we’ve ever seen,” Black Bear president of production & operations Michael Heimler said in a statement. “’They Know’ is authentic, original, and bold filmmaking at the highest level, and we couldn’t be more excited to partner with Bill and re-team with our great friends at MRC, who consistently deliver boundary-pushing films that help define their genre.” Related Stories Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation Watch the ‘Backrooms’ VFX Supervisor Explain His Unique Process of Collaborating with Kane Parsons

Hader co-wrote “They Know” with Duffy Boudreau and produced alongside Bob Graf, with Alyssa Donovan co-producing.

Hader is a three-time Primetime Emmy winner for his work on “South Park” and “Barry.” He co-created the HBO comedy “Barry” with Alec Berg and began directing episodes in Season 2, gradually working his way up to directing the entirety of Season 4. He has long been open about his cinematic influences and his desire to transition into feature filmmaking after the show ended.

Hader recently shared some more details about directing his first feature while speaking at IndieWire’s Los Angeles Future of Filmmaking Summit. He explained that “They Know” emerged after he and longtime friend and writing partner Boudreau both went through divorces and discussed their biggest fears about ways the process could have gone awry.

“We’re both divorced. We were talking about how lucky we were that we were on, like, we had really good terms with our ex-wives, and we have kids with them,” Hader said. “We started talking about the worst case scenarios of, ‘Oh, my god, this person is going through this and this person is going through that.’ And then this idea came up.”

Black Bear has yet to announce a release date for “They Know.”

#3544. DC Names The 1 Villain Darkseid Actually Respects

More often than not, supervillains don’t play well with others, and Darkseid is no exception. As the Lord of Apokolips and the most malevolent of all the New Gods, the entity formerly known as Uxas doesn’t consider anyone to be his equals. Those in his circle are merely a means to an end to achieving his goals, with his minions including Steppenwolf, Granny Goodness, DeSaad, and the mindless Parademons. The few times that Darkseid has joined forces with another powerful antagonist, they’ve been begrudging alliances.

When all is said and done, Darkseid only cares about himself and will sacrifice anyone he deems necessary to further his plans and accumulate more power. Yet, it turns out that there is a popular DC supervillain he actually respects. This is evidenced by Darkseid showing up to literally pay his respects to this newly-deceased troublemaker.

Though the Czarnian bounty hunter Lobo has famously been unkillable, that changed at the end of Lobo #8, when the character’s healing factor was overwhelmed by Francis Damex, the first and last Mauve Lantern. Both Lobo and Francis died during their final battle, and Lobo #9 begins with the Main Man’s funeral underway. Many of DC’s biggest heroes and villains are in attendance for this solemn affair, including Darkseid.

Apokolips’ iron-fisted tyrant is seen standing next to characters like The Joker, Flash, and Sinestro while Maynard, one of the members of Lobo’s unorthodox villain group, gives a funeral sermon for his fallen friend. Amusingly, rather than shedding tears for the late bounty hunter like almost everyone else, Darkseid shoots drooping Omega Beams out of his eyes to show sadness. Maynard also gets bonus points for wearing a hat that says, “New Gods, Who Dis?”, though it’s hard to say if Darkseid approved of this choice in headwear.

Lobo’s funeral was a star-studded affair just like he wanted, but just because he’s dead doesn’t mean he’s gone. Lobo’s ghost is shown observing the event after stealing The Spectre’s cloak, which earns him a walloping from Ted Grant, the current Spectre. Solicitations for the next two Lobo issues confirm that not only will the Main Man get into more shenanigans in the afterlife, but readers will also see more from the team of alternate Lobos, including the much-hated New 52 one who’s now named Chad.

Darkseid and Lobo have rarely crossed paths in the main DC Universe, but the questionable placement of this Lobo series in the canon aside, evidently the former did indeed respect the latter for either professional or personal reasons. It’s a different story when it comes to other realities, though, because Darkseid and Lobo have clashed on three notable occasions in the comics.

In the Injustice universe, Darkseid sent Lobo to Metropolis to hunt down Superman, but the Czarnian later returned to Apokolips to pick a fight with the New God. This initially looked like it would be a suicide mission, as Darkseid doesn’t take kindly to people not carrying out his orders, let alone putting out cigars on his head. Yet, Lobo survived this brawl, though it was left unclear if he defeated Darkseid or if they came to some kind of stalemate.

DC officially kills off and replaces Lobo the same year of his live-action movie debut, only to replace him with a group of very similar characters.

Then, in Tales from the Dark Multiverse: Blackest Night #1, Lobo battled a Nekron-empowered Darkseid. Thanks to his healing factor allowing for even a single drop of blood to regenerate into a new version of himself, Lobo overwhelmed Darkseid with his many duplicates, then gouged out hisses to stop him from using his Omega Beams. Darkseid eventually retreated from their fight, and Lobo’s victory was cemented when he and Sinestro reset the universe.

Additionally, in the DCeased universe, Lobo was immune to the effects of the Anti-Life Virus, and he ended up curing Darkseid of it. Whether there will come a day where the main versions of these two characters have their own showdown is unclear. For now, at least DC fans know that Darkseid thought highly enough of Lobo if he was willing to attend his funeral.

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Free Shadowheart from her pod at the beginning of Baldur’s Gate 3, and she’ll help you get off a crashing mind flayer ship. Ask what she was doing before she got there, and you’ll find out how far rescuing someone actually gets you. Half the fun of those early conversations in the game is deciding when to push your luck with her. It takes a little longer to appreciate how often you’ve asked her a perfectly reasonable question that she couldn’t answer about herself if she wanted to.

Before she met anyone aboard the nautiloid, Shadowheart lived beneath Baldur’s Gate with people who considered a personal history something worth giving up. The cleric has good reason to keep Shar’s secrets by the time you meet her. What’s considerably trickier, as it turns out, is getting another Sharran to tell you theirs when one of your own turns up dead.

Collider can exclusively reveal that Random House Worlds will publish Baldur’s Gate 3: Shadowheart on June 8, 2027. Following Astarion, the publisher’s next prequel comes from Tasha Suri, the World Fantasy Award-winning author of the Burning Kingdoms trilogy. Suri sends Shadowheart from the underground church she calls home to the wealthiest district in Baldur’s Gate, where someone has killed a member of her order. You can get your first look at the cover below.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

Shadowheart has three people to help her work the case, and the one she’d least like to have along is a familiar face. There’s Mirie, a Griefguard with ambitions of her own, and Caldan, whose job as a propagandist hardly inspires confidence in his account of events. Then there’s Nocturne, the quartermistress who insists she’s looking out for Shadowheart. Players who found Nocturne in the House of Grief in Act 3 have some idea how much that assurance means to her. Here, it’s enough to make Shadowheart suspicious.

That’s a hell of a disadvantage to give a detective. Somewhere beneath the city is the Mirror of Loss, where the faithful surrender memories to Shar. Shadowheart believes there’s strength in what she’s given up, but she also has to decide whether to trust a woman who might remember the two of them better than she does. For players who spent hours earning the occasional confidence from Shadowheart, there’s some pleasure in seeing her stuck on the other side of that conversation.

The Upper City complicates the assignment further. It’s the first place in the publisher’s description where Shadowheart sounds like she might actually want to stay. Whatever she finds there, she still has to go home and give an account of herself to the people who sent her. Solving the murder is only half the job when your church also expects you to prove you’re still theirs.

Baldur’s Gate 3: Shadowheart goes on sale June 8, 2027, from Random House Worlds. Stay tuned at Collider for more.

#3542. The Apple Watch's New 'Siri Recap' Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected

The “Siri Recap” feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the “Live Rewind” feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.

I have a button in the watch’s Control Center that can turn the recapping abilities off, but if I forget to do so, Siri listens to everything. I’ll get a recap of my entire evening, presented in roughly hour-long chunks, including things I would have completely forgotten I had even heard about.

The recaps somberly mention silly memes my kids were laughing about, and make major bullet points out of offhand remarks from brief conversations. If a conversation sticks to a single topic, I’ll often get a reasonably good summary of it, with specific facts and numbers highlighted; but just as often, Siri will get confused and mix up several topics or completely mishear a name or phrase.

Apple has four features that it considers part of “audio intelligence":

Music recognition, better known as Shazam. We’ve had a version of this on the Apple Watch for a long time now, although it has some improvements and now identifies music automatically.

Sound recognition, which can notify you about doorbells and babies crying. A version of this launched in 2020 as an accessibility feature.

Live Rewind, which gives you an on-wrist transcript of the last 15 seconds of detected speech.

Siri Recaps, which summarizes entire conversations for you to read on your phone.

Live Rewind had the flashiest demo from the Apple event: A server rattled off the day’s specials at a restaurant, and then the Apple Watch-wearing diner checked his watch to see a readout of exactly which dishes had just been mentioned. The utility is both obvious and kind of unnecessary: Why wouldn’t you just ask the server to repeat the list while they’re standing right there?

I haven’t found myself using Live Rewind, except out of curiosity about how the feature works. I discovered that it doesn’t pick up song lyrics very well, and also that by the time I think to check what was just said in a conversation, more than 15 seconds has passed since the part I was unsure about. I haven’t yet found a reason to use it for real.

But Siri Recaps? Those are both useful and unsettling. I enabled the feature, and decided to test it out later. But since it was on, it dutifully listened in as I picked up my son from school and gave him an update on an ailing family member’s health. We stopped by the library, and along the way we chatted about a variety of things: holiday travel plans, library policies, and the possibility of humans living in space in the future. Siri was listening to it all.

At least for now, the feature is only available in a developer beta, so sign up for that now if you want to try it. You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 (or Ultra 4) and an iPhone 16 or better, excluding the 16e. (I have a 16 Pro, so I'm good.)

After you're updated to 27.3, go into the Watch app, tap Siri, and turn on Siri Recap. You can set a schedule for when it should listen (for example, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., if you want it on for the work day but off for the evening). You'll need to set a passcode on your watch, and you'll be guided through a step to upgrade your audio connection. The control center on the watch will have a button you can use to turn Siri recaps on and off at will. To read your recaps, go to the Siri app on your phone.

But still: I feel weird publishing the contents of these recaps, because they do contain things that people said to me in what they assumed was a private setting. I had the feature on when I attended a choir practice, and Siri recapped the brief chats I had with other choir members before and after practice. (Interestingly, it did not recap any of the quiet conversations I had with fellow sopranos while the tenors were rehearsing their part. I’m not sure if the watch was unable to hear us over the music, or if Siri is programmed not to listen when music is being played.)

Because speakers aren’t identified, it seems Siri doesn’t know what to do when there is a disagreement. A human note-taker would jot down that Person A made a point in favor of something, and person B made a point against. But when my son and I disagreed about how likely space colonization might be in the future, the recap didn’t reflect the separate positions that were put forth. It summarized the conversation as including “debating the feasibility and timeline of human space colonization and asteroid mining,” which isn’t exactly accurate, but close enough.

When it comes to the content of the discussion, the recap notes a bullet point of “skepticism regarding permanent space colonies within the next 100 years.” It didn’t include my reasons for being skeptical, and didn’t mention my son’s opposing viewpoint at all. If I were using this recap to jog my memory of the conversation, it wouldn’t be all that helpful.

Details are sometimes egregiously incorrect. After a discussion about a family member’s health, the recap had notes on the prognosis of “father.” The family member we discussed is not anybody’s father. Names in general seem to be a problem; I recommended a book to my son, and the recap includes notes about the content of the book, but not its title. The book’s author appears in the introduction to the recap (sort of a summary of a summary), but not in the content of the recap itself where the book is mentioned.

I should probably turn Siri recaps off. It seems wrong to let people chat with me without letting them know that their conversation is being ... well, not technically recorded, but basically recorded.

But it’s so tempting to leave it on so that I can review my day. Some of the details in the recaps are useful, like the dates that were discussed as options for a holiday party. The recaps will be deleted in about a week (unless I save them to the notes app), so if I want to remind myself of a conversation a few days ago, I should be able to scroll back through my recaps and find it.

I would be a fool to rely on the recaps, though. The most important points of a conversation are often left out; Siri doesn’t know what’s actually important, and there’s no way to guide it as to what to pay attention to. Specific details can be wrong, as I mentioned. There’s also no way to control when a “conversation” starts or stops, unless you are turning the recap feature on and off from the watch.

And there’s more: Not only are names usually omitted (wait, who did she say I should ask about that project?), the few identifiers that make it into the recap, like names of events, are often wrong. Subjects of discussion are often conflated in really unhelpful ways: My husband mentioned paying for certain course registrations for one of our children, and later I talked to that child about an unrelated exam. The recap got all of these things mixed up with each other and was wrong about pretty much every detail. About all the recap could usefully do is to remind me that something about AP U.S. History was discussed. Reading the recaps can be like reliving your day entirely in the passive voice.

#3541. Apple announces App Store price changes in multiple countries, new California tax rules

Apple today announced that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a new post published on its developer portal, Apple today announced a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the company, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”

Apple added that a new “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and update their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”
