#3400. Anthropic IPO Live — everything you need to know about the $1.5 trillion AI giant

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Anthropic, the AI giant behind Claude, is officially entering an IPO with aggressive stock prices set at $83 share, though it's expected to begin trading at $110 per shared based investor interest.

The company recently reported third quarter revenue of $17 billion, the IPO values the company at trillions more.

At the same time, Anthropic's public stock debut comes at a strange time in the AI industry. Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang just resigned after accusations of affairs and being in a spy web.

AI stocks in general have taken huge hits in the last few weeks. Plus, Anthropic faces major competition from its main rival OpenAI as well as from Google and Meta.

Now the market will determine if Anthropic is as viable as CEO Dario Amodei thinks it is.

Anthropic may be worth more than $2 trillion, but the company behind Claude is offering some businesses discounts of more than 30% to keep them from switching to ChatGPT.

According to a new report from The Information, Anthropic is offering aggressive discounts and credits worth as much as $100,000 to encourage companies to adopt its growing lineup of AI products.

The catch? Some businesses must commit to spending a certain percentage of their overall AI budgets on Anthropic. The company has reportedly started requesting invoices and other documents to verify that customers are meeting those commitments.

It's an interesting strategy for a company celebrating a historic IPO. Claude Code helped Anthropic become a major force in AI, but the company now wants to bring Claude into more workplaces through tools for finance, marketing, human resources and cybersecurity.

That puts Anthropic in direct competition with OpenAI, Microsoft and Google, all fighting for a larger share of corporate AI spending.

For everyday Claude users, these discounts aren't necessarily coming to individual subscriptions. But the competition could eventually mean more capable AI tools and better pricing.

Anthropic now has a massive valuation to justify, and winning over businesses beyond software development could be critical to its next chapter.

Not everyone is celebrating Anthropic's blockbuster IPO. One AI CEO believes the company is making a massive bet on infrastructure that could eventually become obsolete.

David Stout, co-founder and CEO of webAI, is questioning Anthropic's valuation after the company priced its IPO at $83 per share.

"Anthropic's IPO asks public investors to bet that the future of AI belongs to whoever spends the most to centralize it," Stout said in a statement shared with Amanda Caswell.

His biggest concern is Anthropic's nearly $900 billion in computing and infrastructure commitments, some extending through 2045.

Stout argues that cloud-based AI becomes more expensive as people use it more, while AI running directly on phones, laptops and other devices could eventually offer a cheaper alternative.

"Anthropic is asking investors to pour billions into an infrastructure model that AI itself is making obsolete," he said.

There's an important catch to his argument. Smaller AI models are becoming more capable, but running the most powerful models locally still presents significant technical challenges.

For investors, the debate raises a question about Anthropic's future. Can the company generate enough demand for Claude to justify decades of infrastructure spending, or will cheaper alternatives eventually change the economics of AI?

Anthropic just became one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies. But does its enormous valuation mean Claude is better than ChatGPT?

The answer depends on what you're asking AI to do. Claude has built a strong reputation among developers, particularly through Claude Code, which can help write, debug and work with code across software projects.

It's also a popular choice for writing, analyzing documents and working through complex problems.

ChatGPT, meanwhile, offers an extensive collection of consumer-facing features, including image generation, voice conversations, research tools and coding capabilities through Codex.

Both companies are continually releasing new models and features, making it difficult to declare one chatbot the overall winner.

And Anthropic's IPO valuation isn't a measurement of Claude's intelligence. But it does reflect what investors are willing to pay for a stake in the business and their expectations about its future growth.

Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT or Claude, many people use these tools interchangeably, so the question isn't which one is better, but how can I best use each one.

Anthropic's blockbuster IPO is a major moment for the AI industry, but it also raises a question that has nothing to do with the stock market. If AI is becoming so powerful, what does this mean for the future of work?

The company behind Claude is developing technology that can already write code, analyze documents, conduct research and complete tasks that previously required human employees. And Anthropic's own research offers an interesting glimpse into how that could change the workplace.

In a recent study of its employees, the company found that coding-focused AI agent sessions among nontechnical workers increased dramatically, from two per month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026.

The research also found signs of slowing junior employment in roles that use Claude for particularly complex tasks, although that doesn't establish that AI caused the slowdown.

Anthropic's IPO gives the company additional resources to expand its models and workplace tools. For employees, that could mean more opportunities to automate repetitive work, but it also raises concerns about which tasks companies will continue paying people to perform.

As we know, AI has already entered the workplace, so for now, it's about how quickly businesses adopt these tools and whether workers benefit from the productivity gains.

Anthropic just became a $2 trillion company, but does that mean Claude users should expect to pay more? Not necessarily.

For now, Anthropic's IPO doesn't automatically change the price of a Claude subscription.

Claude still offers a free version, while its Pro subscription costs $20 per month, or about $17 per month with annual billing. The company also offers higher-priced plans for people who need more extensive access to its AI models.

However, running powerful AI systems is expensive. Every conversation, coding session and complex research task requires computing resources.

As a public company, Anthropic will face greater scrutiny over its revenue, expenses and ability to become sustainably profitable.

That could influence future decisions about subscriptions, usage limits and premium features, although there's no evidence that the IPO itself will trigger an immediate price increase.

What might happen, is competitors might offer more, for less. ChatGPT already offers unlimited chatting, but we might see more Pro options among the free tier. This is something to watch for from Anthropic's biggest competitors.

Anthropic's historic IPO is attracting enormous excitement from investors, but buried in the company's financial disclosures is a warning about the technology making it so valuable.

Advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic warned in its IPO filing.

It's a striking admission from a company seeking billions of dollars from investors to develop increasingly powerful AI systems.

Anthropic has long positioned itself as a company focused on AI safety. Its founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, previously worked at OpenAI before launching their own AI research company in 2021.

But even Anthropic acknowledges that testing advanced AI models has limitations. In its IPO prospectus, the company warned that AI systems could develop unexpected capabilities during training, and that some potential dangers might not become apparent until after deployment.

These aren't predictions that an AI disaster is inevitable, but they are risks the company believes investors need to understand. For users like you and me, the warning highlights the challenges facing AI developers as chatbots become more capable than ever of taking actions, writing software and handling sensitive information.

Anthropic's IPO is a financial milestone, but its safety disclosures are a reminder that the technology's long-term consequences remain uncertain.OpenAI said they waited to file IPO for safety reasons.

Claude might be best known as a ChatGPT competitor, but Anthropic's biggest opportunity may be inside the workplace.

According to the company's IPO prospectus, more than half of Fortune 500 companies were Anthropic customers generating at least $100,000 in revenue over the preceding 12 months as of September 30, 2026.

Anthropic also reported more than 1,900 customers generating at least $1 million in revenue over the same period, along with approximately 250 generating $10 million or more.

Those numbers offer a glimpse into why investors are willing to value the company so highly.

Businesses are using Claude for everything from software development to document analysis, insurance underwriting and cybersecurity. Unlike a consumer paying $20 per month for Claude Pro, large organizations can spend millions annually as they expand their use of AI.

Anthropic's success with Claude Code has also helped it establish a strong foothold among developers.

For everyday users, this is important because the next generation of Claude features may focus more on work rather than casual conversations like a typical chatbot.

#3399. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

#3397. Catch Electronics Shock and Drop Failures Before Hardware Is Built

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3392. UK court rules Apple can share the top secret order everyone already knew

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.

Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the issue …

In 2025, the British government ordered Apple to create a backdoor to allow access by security services and law enforcement. Even worse, the order was issued under legislation that prohibits companies from revealing that they have received this demand.

This would have meant that British customers who enabled ADP would think that their data was safe when in fact it wasn’t. As we’ve said many times before, any backdoor created for use by the good guys is vulnerable to discovery and exploitation by the bad guys.

“Apple can no longer offer Advanced Data Protection (ADP) in the United Kingdom to new users and current UK users will eventually need to disable this security feature. ADP protects iCloud data with end-to-end encryption, which means the data can only be decrypted by the user who owns it, and only on their trusted devices. We are gravely disappointed that the protections provided by ADP will not be available to our customers in the UK […] As we have said many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will.”

Tell me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP without telling me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP …

The UK government must admit that it issued a secret order to Apple to allow it access to encrypted customer data, a court has ruled […] The Home Office has “not established that it would be damaging to national security” to reveal that Apple had received a “technical capability notice” (TCN), the tribunal said. The ruling means that […] “much” of Apple and the non-profits’ legal challenge can now take place in open court.

One of the great ironies is that most people had never heard of ADP until the government effectively made it headline news in the tech press three years after it launched – a classic example of the Streisand Effect.

This ruling is a win both for transparency and commonsense. To be clear, the actual requirement for a backdoor remains in place, but this can now be challenged in open court.

Gordon Ramsay and Claudia Winkleman are reopening the doors to Hell’s Kitchen in the UK.

The presenters will front a reboot of the cooking format more than 20 years after it originally premiered on ITV in 2004. The show will return in 2027, opening a Michelin-standard restaurant for two weeks, staffed by 10 celebrity contestants.

Hell’s Kitchen will be co-produced by Lifted Entertainment (part of ITV Studios), which created the format, and Studio Ramsay Global.

#3388. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3387. iOS 27.3 beta can cause HomeView issues, Apple confirms

Apple’s new HomeView just launched last Friday, but some early adopters reported issues with Siri AI in their first days of use. Apple shipped fixes in HomeView 27.2.1 yesterday, but it also confirmed the iOS 27.3 beta is responsible for some of the problems.

Yesterday Apple released its first post-launch software update for HomeView, less than a week after the product debuted.

Per the company’s official release notes, HomeView 27.2.1 focuses on bug fixes, including a fix for the following issue:

Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail

It’s unknown how many reports of Siri issues on HomeView can be attributed to the iOS 27.3 beta. However, it wouldn’t surprise me if many of the reports were from beta users. That’s in part because early HomeView reviewers didn’t seem to have the same problems.

With HomeView 27.2.1 now available, those problems should hopefully be taken care of. However, if you’re on the iOS 27.3 beta, there’s a new issue you’ll need to deal with temporarily.

As discovered by pdfu, if you try to make a Personal Content request on an iPhone running iOS 27.3, Siri in HomeView 27.2.1 now says: “I can’t help with that because your personal device is on newer software.”

If you’re on iOS 27.3, Siri on HomeView can’t use your iPhone for personal context, likely until December.HomeView won’t send Siri requests to an iPhone on newer software. Without a HomeView update, your only option is iOS 27.2.x.On-device requests like timers still work. https://t.co/8UbRs7z496

It’s understandable that issues might arise from having iOS and HomeView software that’s out of sync. Unfortunately though, there’s no beta software available for HomeView at the moment.

That means unless Apple releases a beta soon, users might have to wait until the public launch of HomeView 27.3 in December to get Personal Content features back.

How has Siri AI been working for you on HomeView? Let us know in the comments.

#3385. Fremantle Group COO Andrea Scrosati Exiting After Eight Years

Andrea Scrosati is leaving Got Talent and Baywatch producer Fremantle after eight years to launch “a new entrepreneurial venture.”

The exec will stay in his role as Fremantle Group COO and CEO of Continental Europe until the end of January 2027. Announcement of his exit comes three days after Deadline revealed Fremantle U.S. COO Suzanne Lopez was leaving after 23 years.

Scrosati has been with Fremantle since 2018, having joined from Sky Italia. Initially group COO, he added Continential Europe to his duties in 2021. Notably, he led Fremantle’s M&A strategy and led the acquisitions of Poor Things producer Element Pictures, Asacha Media Group and Costiera maker Lux Video. He also backed pushes into the FAST channel business and AI, notably spearheading the creation Imaginae Studios, whose first production, Art Awakens, launched this year. Related Stories News 'American Idol' Gets Rid Of Hollywood Week In Favor Of More Live Shows As ABC Music Competition Moves To Georgia: "Major Changes Coming" Executives Fremantle U.S. COO Suzanne Lopez Exiting After Over 20 Years

The Italian exec also backed Fremantle’s push into global film, with the company delivering its 100th feature this year. The strategy was expensive and in March, Fremantle parent RTL Group announced Fremantle would no longer fully finance films following a review. Watch on Deadline

Scrosati can point to four Academy Awards and 17 Academy nominations, the Golden Lion at Venice and awards in Cannes and Berlin as an answer to Fremantle’s critics.

“Andrea has made an enormous contribution to Fremantle over the past eight years,” said Fremantle CEO Jennifer Mullin. “He has been instrumental in our growth and transformation, from helping build Fremantle into a true portfolio company and leading our M&A strategy, to establishing our film strategy and constantly pushing us to think differently about innovation and the future of our business.

“Just as importantly, Andrea has been a trusted colleague, partner and a great friend to me. I will miss working alongside him enormously, but I’m incredibly excited for him as he takes this next entrepreneurial step. I’m grateful that he has agreed to stay with us through the end of January to support the transition, and I know everyone at Fremantle joins me in wishing him every success in this new adventure.”

“These eight years at Fremantle have been an extraordinary privilege,” added Scrosati. “Fremantle is a unique company, with incredible people, some of the world’s finest creative talent and an exceptional portfolio of IP. I leave with enormous pride in what we have achieved together and great affection for the company and everyone who makes it what it is. The time feels right for me to take the next step and focus on building something new.

“I want to thank Jen for her leadership, vision and trust, all my colleagues across Fremantle, and RTL Group and Bertelsmann for their unwavering support over the years. Fremantle has an exciting future ahead, and I look forward to working with the team over the coming months to ensure a smooth transition.”

#3383. Microsoft To Do is retiring, including Mac and iOS apps

Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know.

The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

“Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly says it has no plans for a native Mac app.

You can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft plans to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the company.

The June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

#3380. International Insider: Pattinson Becomes Bond; SkyShowtime Shutting Down; The Brit List

We’re shaken and stirred after this week in film and TV, Insiders. Jesse Whittock with you to recall events as the world was introduced to the latest James Bond.

“Welcome to the world’s most exclusive club”: And now we know the identity of the next 007. Robert Pattinson is stepping into the well-heeled shoes of James Bond and will star in the next three films from the spy franchise. Pattinson beat out competition from the likes of Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor after emerging as one of the five Deadline revealed a few weeks back would test for the iconic role. The decision was immediately divisive: Many people believe Pattinson has the look and the acting chops to do a great job with Bond, while many others feel he’s probably too well-established already (he is the current Batman!) for a role that has broadly made stars of relative unknowns. Baz Bamigboye’s wonderful column on the casting summed it up, including a quote from a feature film biz source who groaned, “Bond is mysterious. Bond creates the stars. The stars don’t create Bond… For f*ck’s sake!” In the end, Denis Villeneuve went for an actor he knows and trusts – Pattinson will soon be seen in the Canadian director’s Dune: Part Three. The revelation that Amazon boss Jeff Bezos played a large role in the selection didn’t go down well below the line, with one commenter writing, “Pretty awful seeing the fate of James Bond in the hands of a real-life Bond villain.” Since Amazon bought the Broccoli family out of the Bond franchise, there has been industry chatter that the tech and streaming giant would need a bona fide star – someone seriously bankable – to recoup the massive outlay. In R-Patz, they’ve certainly got that: he’s acted in everything from the Twilight movies to Christopher Nolan’s Tenet through to The Batman, and much-loved indie pics such as The Lighthouse and this year’s Primetime, as Dessi Gomez’s gallery item shows. Villeneuve is now designing Bond’s next assignment, but we don’t know when exactly the first Pattinson film is coming. For now, the newest spy on the block should grab a minute to take it all in, say Bond’s of years past. “Welcome to the world’s most exclusive club, but remember to enjoy yourself,” On Her Majesty’s Secret Service star George Lazenby told Pattinson in a sweet video in the hours after the biggest casting news of the year. Related Stories Casting Pierce Brosnan Bonds With Robert Pattinson Over 007 Role News 'Primetime' Cinematographer & Editor On Making Robert Pattinson Look Like A "Superhero" & Breakdown Viral Meme Catchphrase

Accountability demanded: It’s been a traumatic few weeks in the British entertainment industry. First, Russell Brand was found guilty of sex crimes, followed by revelations about David Walliams’ alleged conduct. Former Doctor Who actor Noel Clarke was also in court this week. He will stand trial next year after pleading not guilty to five sex offence charges. The UK industry is facing a reckoning, and this week a group of actors and other creatives – including Natalie Dormer, Richard Armitage and Susan Wokoma – signed an open letter demanding an end to a “culture of open secrets” in the entertainment industry. The letter called out broadcasters, studios, indies, industry organizations and unions, urging them to review processes, protect whistleblowers and those speaking out, and to “become less offended by your inaction being named than you are by the actions you are being asked to recognize.”

Digging it: Another group of young British writing hopefuls had their moment in the sun this week as the latest Brit List of yet-to-be-produced film and TV screenplays was announced. Topping the pile was Gemmy Addy’s coming-of-age feature script Dig For Victory and Archie Thomson’s Cornish crime series Petroc, both of which got 25 industry recommendations. We once again partnered with The Brit List to bring you interviews with the writers, with Addy telling us her grandmother’s World War II experiences inspired her story and Thomson attributing his script’s success to influence from England’s West County… and Taylor Sheridan. Black Friday is an excellent time to score a new pair of headphones that would otherwise be a splurge, with retailers like Amazon and Walmart already offering massive discounts on tech essentials from top brands a week ahead of the holiday. One of the early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar is the Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones, a mid-range noise-canceling option that’s perfect for bass lovers and is currently 50% off, dropping to $119.99 (originally $239.99).

PCMag says they deliver “brain-rattling levels of bass” and have a comfortable fit, with generous memory foam cushioning and minimal clamping pressure that lends itself well to long listening sessions. The aesthetic is nothing to scoff at either, with a refined and modern style. It’s worth noting they also come in a hardshell zip-up case with a fabric-lined exterior.

Powered by 40mm dynamic drivers, they offer reliable noise cancellation with the ANC slider set to max on the companion app, which lets users adjust a range of controls and listening modes, including the intensity of bass. #3378. iPadOS 27.3: Three new features coming to your iPad

iPadOS 27.3 is now in beta and will launch to all users next month, here are three new features it introduces for iPad.

There’s a new setting in iPadOS 27.3 that I instantly turned on and have been loving. It lets you double-tap the top of a window to resize it.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if ‘Windowed Apps’ is enabled there’s now a new toggle: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom.’

I’ve been using this gesture all the time in the beta, because it lets me resize my window to fullscreen then revert it to its previous size with ease. It’s an intuitive, convenient way to resize windows for different tasks.

Read more: iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on

Visual intelligence was available on iPad already, but iPadOS 27.3 adds a dedicated hub for using the feature: a new Siri mode in the Camera app.

iOS 27 brought Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app, but it was missing from iPad. iPadOS 27.3 corrects that oversight, letting you use your iPad’s built-in Camera app to ask Siri about any object you capture.

Baking visual intelligence into Camera should expose the feature to a lot more iPad users, since before you had to set up a custom control or shortcut for it. And with how much better visual intelligence has gotten thanks to Siri AI, the Siri mode is a valuable addition.

Read more: iOS 27 gives the Camera app on iPhone a brand new mode

Freeform is gaining a variety of new features in iPadOS 27.3. They’re available in macOS and iOS too, but out of all Apple platforms, Freeform feels very much built for the iPad.

Which iPadOS 27.3 features are you most looking forward to? Let us know in the comments.

#3374. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3370. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

Discover how Innomotics is driving the future of industry: https://www.innomotics.com/hub/en/company/about-innomotics/dynamo-electric-principle

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

#3369. Halide camera app just got even better for iPhone Duo

Halide 3.4 is out today as the latest update to the pro camera app. The update adds several new features, including a larger viewfinder for iPhone Duo and more.

The new Halide update also lets you use the outer screen on iPhone Duo as a live preview or a fill flash. It brings back a few camera tools from Halide Mark II as well.

Lux Optics first added iPhone Duo support in October with Halide 3.3. With the phone fully open, the initial iPhone Duo update let you review your most recent photo alongside the live viewfinder.

Today’s new XL mode gives you the option to swap the photo preview for a larger viewfinder. Controls on both sides enable two-handed shooting.

While the Duo is open, the outer screen can mirror Halide’s camera controls or show a full-screen viewfinder without controls. The second option lets the person you’re photographing see how you’ve framed the shot.

In low light, Halide can use the outer screen as a fill flash. That gives you a softer source of light for portraits, and Halide’s developers recommend turning the screen brightness all the way up before taking the photo.

Halide also now places the histogram along the Duo’s crease. The update revises the Photo Lab interface for editing with the Duo half open as well.

On other iPhones, Halide 3.4 restores the color and luminance histograms and the shutter timer from Mark II.

Halide Mark III launched back in May with a redesigned camera and the new Photo Lab editor. Recent updates added RAW-only capture in 3.1 and Aperture Priority for iPhone 18 Pro in 3.2. Halide Mark III version 3.4 is available now on the App Store.

#3368. The Best Early Black Friday Smart Home Deals

Amazon's early Black Friday 2026 sale is already bringing some substantial discounts on smart home devices, with savings ranging from $23 to $700 across security cameras, video doorbells, smart locks, home security systems, thermostats, and robot vacuums. Several products are more than 50% off, including indoor security cameras from Blink, Ring, and Arlo, while higher-end devices from Eufy and Roborock are seeing price cuts of hundreds of dollars.

You can also check out our other Black Friday coverage for more tech deals as the sale continues. For now, here are some of the best early Black Friday 2026 smart home deals worth checking out.

Named the best security camera of 2024 by PCMag, TP-Link’s Tapo MagCam C425 is now down to $54.99 from $89.99, making it an affordable option for keeping an eye on your driveway, backyard, or front entrance without having to run power cables. It records in 2K resolution and runs on a rechargeable battery, while support for microSD storage lets you save footage locally without paying for a cloud subscription.

Reolink’s 4K Solar Security Camera is down to $144.99 from $229.99, saving you $85. It connects over 4G LTE, so it can keep watch over a barn, vacation home, construction sites, or other areas where a regular wifi security camera won't work because there’s no home network to join. Its microSD support lets you save footage locally without a cloud subscription—you will, however, need an active cellular data plan to get the camera online.

Eufy’s SoloCam S340 is $119.99, down from $219.99, and it pairs a 3K wide-angle lens with a 2K telephoto lens, giving you a view of the whole yard and a closer look at faces or packages at the same time. The camera pans a full 360 degrees and tilts to follow people as they move, and the included solar panel keeps it charged in a sunny spot. Footage is stored on 8GB of built-in storage with no monthly fee—one of the reasons why the S340 earned an Editors’ Choice award in PCMag’s review.

Eufy’s Video Doorbell E340 is $99.99, down from $169.99, and it uses two cameras to cover your front door, with one recording visitors in 2K and the other pointing down at the doorstep to keep an eye on deliveries. It also has color night vision, a removable rechargeable battery, and 8GB of built-in storage for recording footage without a cloud subscription. You can read more about its performance in PCMag's review.

At $28, down from $79.99, the second-generation Arlo Wireless Video Doorbell 2K is one of the more affordable ways to keep an eye on your front door. Its 2K camera provides a detailed view of visitors, while the wide field of view helps capture packages left near your doorstep—making it easy to see why PCMag named it the best video doorbell of 2024.

The Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ is down to $34.99 from $79.99. It records in 2K resolution and offers a head-to-toe view, so you can see who's at the door as well as any packages left on your doorstep. And since it runs on batteries, installation is relatively simple, especially for renters or anyone who doesn't want to deal with doorbell wiring. For more on it, check out PCMag’s review.

The Eufy Security FamiLock E34 is down to $179.99 from $279.99, saving you $100 on a smart lock that uses palm vein recognition to unlock your door, which Eufy says takes just 0.6 seconds. It can store palm data for up to 50 people locally, making it convenient for households with multiple users, while PIN codes and app-based controls give you other ways to get inside. You also get built-in wifi and compatibility with Apple Home, Alexa, Google Home, and Matter.

The Ultraloq Bolt Fingerprint smart lock is $139.99, down from $199.99, and it replaces your deadbolt with a lock you can open using a fingerprint, a keypad code, or the U Home app over built-in wifi. It can also unlock automatically as you walk up to the door, using your phone’s location. PCMag named it the best smart lock of 2024.

SimpliSafe’s DIY 8-piece Wireless Home Security System is down to $119.99 from $209.99, making it a relatively affordable starting point for securing multiple entry points around your home. The kit includes a base station, keypad, entry sensors, a motion sensor, and a panic button, so you can monitor doors, windows, and movement inside the house. For more details, check out PCMag’s in-depth review.

The Arlo Home Security System is $142.49, down from $199.99, and this starter kit pairs a Keypad Sensor Hub with two All-in-One Sensors, each of which can be set to detect motion, open doors and windows, water leaks, and other events across eight functions. It runs in the same Arlo Secure app as Arlo’s cameras and doorbells, which makes it a natural addition for homes that already use them. For more on its features and performance, check out PCMag’s review.

At just $15.99, down from $39.99, the Blink Mini 2K+ is one of the cheapest ways to add indoor monitoring to your smart home. This compact plug-in camera records in 2K resolution, and also supports motion alerts, two-way audio, and Alexa integration. PCMag has a review of the Blink Mini 2K+.

Arlo’s Essential Pan Tilt Indoor Cam 2K is $18.99, down from $49.99, and it’s part of the lineup Arlo released in 2025, with a motorized head that rotates a full 360 degrees and tilts 180 degrees so one camera can cover an entire room. This PCMag review goes into more detail on how it performs.

The Sensi Smart Thermostat ST55 is currently $79, down from $129.99, and is a good option for anyone looking to control their home's heating and cooling from a phone—it lets you create schedules, adjust temperatures remotely, and use geofencing to make changes based on whether you're home or away. It also works with several popular smart home platforms, including Alexa, Google Assistant, and Samsung SmartThings, plus Apple HomeKit when a C-wire is connected, notes this PCMag review.

The Amazon Smart Thermostat is a more affordable alternative at $56.99, down from $79.99. It works with Alexa to let you adjust temperatures through voice commands or the Alexa app, where you can also set schedules and automate temperature changes based on your routines. For more on its setup and features, check out PCMag's review.

Ecovacs’ Deebot X8 Pro Omni is down to $699.99 from $1,099.99, saving you $400 on a robot vacuum that takes care of both vacuuming and mopping. It uses a roller mop that continuously rinses itself with clean water as it works and extends outward to clean along walls and furniture. You also get 18,000Pa of suction and a self-maintaining dock that empties the dustbin, washes the mop with hot water, and dries it afterward. For more on its cleaning performance, check out PCMag’s review.

The Roborock Qrevo CurvX has dropped to $799.99 from $1,499.99, saving you $700. It’s a 2025 update to the Qrevo Curv that raises suction from 18,500Pa to 22,000Pa and slims the robot to 3.14 inches tall so it fits under more couches and beds, while keeping the AdaptiLift chassis for climbing thresholds and a dock that washes the mop pads with hot water. This PCMag review covers the original Qrevo Curv, which should be a useful reference for the design and dock the two models share.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.
